items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a coherent world view that responds to an issue and is made up of argument, evidence and assumptions, shaped by a particular standpoint”?
items.answer: Perspective
items.markingKey: Perspective: a coherent world view that responds to an issue and is made up of argument, evidence and assumptions, shaped by a particular standpoint. [1]

items.stem: On the issue of the under-representation of women in parliaments, UN Women supports temporary special measures such as quotas. Which is the most likely reason for this perspective?
options: He wants to protect his reputation and position
It works for gender equality under SDG 5
Regulation would raise its costs and legal risks
It believes not voting is a legitimate choice and the state should not coerce citizens
items.answer: It works for gender equality under SDG 5
items.markingKey: UN Women: it works for gender equality under SDG 5. [1]

items.stem: On the issue of state use of facial recognition surveillance, a police chief supports facial recognition. Which is the most likely reason for this perspective?
options: Such laws have been used to jail journalists
He believes quotas restrict local members’ choice
She believes it helps catch dangerous offenders
items.answer: She believes it helps catch dangerous offenders
items.markingKey: A police chief: she believes it helps catch dangerous offenders. [1]

items.stem: On the issue of threats to press freedom, a government spokesperson argues restrictions protect national security, while a citizen who relies on state television trusts official news. Identify the two perspectives described.
items.answer: A government spokesperson: argues restrictions protect national security. A citizen who relies on state television: trusts official news.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: On the issue of the spread of online disinformation during elections, an electoral commission wants transparency rules for online political adverts, while a social media company prefers voluntary codes of conduct to new laws. (a) Identify the two perspectives described. (b) Explain one factor that might influence the perspective of a social media company.
items.answer: (a) An electoral commission: wants transparency rules for online political adverts. A social media company: prefers voluntary codes of conduct to new laws. (b) Regulation would raise its costs and legal risks; it may also be shaped by its values, role or interests.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark factor; 1 mark linked to view [2]

items.stem: On the issue of threats to press freedom, a citizen who relies on state television trusts official news, while a government spokesperson argues restrictions protect national security. (a) Identify the two perspectives described. (b) Suggest how a feminist perspective might differ from both.
items.answer: (a) A citizen who relies on state television: trusts official news. A government spokesperson: argues restrictions protect national security. (b) A feminist perspective values equality between women and men and challenging patriarchal structures, so it would ask whether the response advances or ignores gender equality.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark values; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: Assess the claim that people’s perspectives on the under-representation of women in parliaments are shaped more by self-interest than by values.
items.answer: For: UN Women supports temporary special measures such as quotas because it works for gender equality under SDG 5. Organisations with vested interests often adopt views that protect them. Against: Some actors are driven by principle, e.g. a party official: he believes quotas restrict local members’ choice. Ideologies such as liberalism or socialism shape views even when they cost the holder. Judgement: Interests and values usually combine; a supported judgement uses examples of each and considers how far they can be separated.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: An article written for the government imposing sanctions argues that it argues they punish aggression on the question of the use of economic sanctions, noting that it wants to show strength without military action. Explain why it is important to know who produced this statement when judging its perspective.
items.answer: The perspective reflects the producer’s position: it wants to show strength without military action. Knowing this reveals possible vested interest or bias, so the reader can judge how far the view is balanced and look for other perspectives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies who/position; 1 mark explains interest or purpose; 1 mark effect on how we judge the view [3]

items.stem: Daniel argues that on the export of plastic waste to poorer countries, the perspective of the government of an exporting country is more convincing than the perspective of an environmental NGO in Malaysia. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence. You may wish to consider: vested interests; national and global perspectives.
items.answer: For: The government of an exporting country claims its waste is recycled responsibly: it wants to meet recycling targets cheaply. Its view may be supported by evidence about the consequences of the issue. Against: An environmental NGO in Malaysia calls for a total ban on imports: it sees local communities harmed. Each perspective may be influenced by vested interest; independent evidence is needed. Judgement: A supported judgement compares the reasoning, evidence and possible bias of each perspective rather than simply agreeing with one.

Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a connected set of political ideas about how society should be organised”?
items.answer: Ideology
items.markingKey: Ideology: a connected set of political ideas about how society should be organised. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a citizen who relies on state television might take a different perspective on threats to press freedom from other stakeholders.
items.answer: Its perspective is shaped by its position and interests: she has little access to alternative sources. Other stakeholders, e.g. a government spokesperson, have different interests or values, so they reach a different view.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the influence (interest, values, experience, role); 1 mark explains link to the view; 1 mark contrast with another stakeholder [3]

items.stem: The education ministry proposes to run citizenship education programmes in schools. Explain how someone with a feminist perspective might judge this proposal.
items.answer: A feminist perspective values equality between women and men and challenging patriarchal structures, so they would judge the proposal by whether it advances or ignores gender equality. Depending on that, they could support it or oppose it; e.g. the limitation “results take years to appear and depend on teaching quality” may matter more or less to them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies core values of the perspective; 1 mark applies them to the proposal; 1 mark reaches a reasoned likely response [3]

items.stem: On the issue of migration caused by climate change, UNHCR recognises climate change as a driver of displacement but uses the existing definition of a refugee, while the government of a low-lying Pacific island state demands that high-emitting countries accept responsibility. Suggest how a conservative perspective might differ from both.
items.answer: A conservative perspective values tradition, order, stability and gradual change, so it would ask whether the response preserves stability and established institutions or risks sudden disruption.
items.markingKey: 1 mark values; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: On the issue of migration caused by climate change, a populist party in a high-income country opposes new obligations to accept migrants, while UNHCR recognises climate change as a driver of displacement but uses the existing definition of a refugee. Explain one factor that might influence the perspective of UNHCR.
items.answer: It must work within the mandate states have given it; it may also be shaped by its values, role or interests.
items.markingKey: 1 mark factor; 1 mark linked to view [2]

items.stem: On the issue of corruption in public procurement, a government minister accused of corruption claims the investigation is politically motivated, while a business association supports simpler procurement rules. Suggest how a liberal perspective might differ from both.
items.answer: A liberal perspective values individual freedom, rights and limited, accountable government, so it would ask whether the response protects or restricts individual rights and freedoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark values; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: “People’s perspectives on corruption in public procurement are shaped more by self-interest than by values.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Transparency International campaigns for open contracting and stronger enforcement because it is an NGO whose mission is to fight corruption. Organisations with vested interests often adopt views that protect them. Against: Some actors are driven by principle, e.g. a business association: complex rules raise costs for its members. Ideologies such as liberalism or socialism shape views even when they cost the holder. Judgement: Interests and values usually combine; a supported judgement uses examples of each and considers how far they can be separated.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that people’s perspectives on state use of facial recognition surveillance are shaped more by self-interest than by values.
items.answer: For: A police chief supports facial recognition because she believes it helps catch dangerous offenders. Organisations with vested interests often adopt views that protect them. Against: Some actors are driven by principle, e.g. a civil liberties group: it defends privacy and freedom of assembly. Ideologies such as liberalism or socialism shape views even when they cost the holder. Judgement: Interests and values usually combine; a supported judgement uses examples of each and considers how far they can be separated.

Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the reason a source was produced, for example to inform, persuade or sell”?
items.answer: Purpose of a source
items.markingKey: Purpose of a source: the reason a source was produced, for example to inform, persuade or sell. [1]

items.stem: A spokesperson for a student union told a press conference in Lisbon that the organisation supports voting at 16, explaining that its members are directly affected. Explain why it is important to know who produced this statement when judging its perspective.
items.answer: The perspective reflects the producer’s position: its members are directly affected. Knowing this reveals possible vested interest or bias, so the reader can judge how far the view is balanced and look for other perspectives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies who/position; 1 mark explains interest or purpose; 1 mark effect on how we judge the view [3]

items.stem: An article written for the government of an exporting country argues that it claims its waste is recycled responsibly on the question of the export of plastic waste to poorer countries, noting that it wants to meet recycling targets cheaply. Explain why it is important to know who produced this statement when judging its perspective.
items.answer: The perspective reflects the producer’s position: it wants to meet recycling targets cheaply. Knowing this reveals possible vested interest or bias, so the reader can judge how far the view is balanced and look for other perspectives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies who/position; 1 mark explains interest or purpose; 1 mark effect on how we judge the view [3]

items.stem: Read the source. “Speaking at a conference in Hanoi on the under-representation of women in parliaments, a representative of a female MP elected through a quota said that it argues quotas opened doors that had been closed.” Identify a stakeholder likely to hold a different perspective, and explain why.
items.answer: UN Women, which supports temporary special measures such as quotas, because it works for gender equality under SDG 5.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stakeholder; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Read the source. “In a statement published on its website, the government of Egypt says it fears reduced Nile flows. The statement adds that it depends on the Nile for most of its fresh water.” (a) Identify who holds this perspective. (b) Identify a stakeholder likely to hold a different perspective, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) The government of Egypt. (b) The government of Ethiopia, which argues the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is vital for development, because millions of its people lack electricity.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark stakeholder; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Source A: In a statement published on its website, the targeted government says it calls the sanctions illegal interference. The statement adds that it wants to blame external enemies for economic problems. Source B: In a statement published on its website, the government imposing sanctions says it argues they punish aggression. The statement adds that it wants to show strength without military action. (a) Identify the perspective in each source. (b) Explain which source is more likely to be influenced by a vested interest.
items.answer: (a) A: the targeted government calls the sanctions illegal interference. B: the government imposing sanctions argues they punish aggression. (b) The one whose producer gains or loses directly (money, power, reputation) from the outcome; judgement must be explained using provenance.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark choice; 1 mark identifies interest; 1 mark explains effect on reliability [3]

items.stem: What is meant by “global perspective” in Global Perspectives?
options: Combining insights from different perspectives into a new, more complete understanding.
A view that considers how an issue affects people across the world and the shared interests involved.
Points on which different perspectives agree.
items.answer: A view that considers how an issue affects people across the world and the shared interests involved.
items.markingKey: Global perspective: a view that considers how an issue affects people across the world and the shared interests involved. [1]

items.stem: On lowering the voting age to 16, a conservative columnist opposes lowering the age, while a student union supports voting at 16. Identify one difference and one possible similarity between these perspectives.
items.answer: Difference: they reach opposite or different conclusions, because she believes adulthood and full rights should start at 18 whereas its members are directly affected. Possible similarity: both accept that lowering the voting age to 16 is a real issue that needs a response.
items.markingKey: 1 mark difference; 1 mark explained; 1 mark plausible similarity [3]

items.stem: On corruption in public procurement, Transparency International campaigns for open contracting and stronger enforcement, while a business association supports simpler procurement rules. Identify one difference and one possible similarity between these perspectives.
items.answer: Difference: they reach opposite or different conclusions, because it is an NGO whose mission is to fight corruption whereas complex rules raise costs for its members. Possible similarity: both accept that corruption in public procurement is a real issue that needs a response.
items.markingKey: 1 mark difference; 1 mark explained; 1 mark plausible similarity [3]

items.stem: Perspective 1: Reporters Without Borders condemns the restrictions. Perspective 2: A government spokesperson argues restrictions protect national security. Both concern threats to press freedom. Explain why each group holds its perspective.
items.answer: 1: it is an NGO that defends press freedom. 2: the government wants to limit critical coverage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: An opinion poll in Dravonia asked whether the exporting governments should ban exports and build domestic recycling capacity. Group | Urban | Rural | Small towns | Suburbs. % supporting | 38% | 60% | 75% | 67%. Calculate the difference in support between the most and least supportive groups, and suggest why their perspectives might differ.
items.answer: 37 percentage points (Small towns 75% vs Urban 38%). The groups may be affected differently by the proposal or hold different values and interests.
items.markingKey: 1 mark groups identified; 1 mark difference in percentage points; 1 mark plausible reason linked to interests/experience [3]

items.stem: Arjun argues that on the under-representation of women in parliaments, the perspective of a female MP elected through a quota is more convincing than the perspective of a party official. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence. You may wish to consider: vested interests; the quality of evidence.
items.answer: For: A female MP elected through a quota argues quotas opened doors that had been closed: she has personal experience of the selection process. Its view may be supported by evidence about the consequences of the issue. Against: A party official prefers selection “on merit”: he believes quotas restrict local members’ choice. Each perspective may be influenced by vested interest; independent evidence is needed. Judgement: A supported judgement compares the reasoning, evidence and possible bias of each perspective rather than simply agreeing with one.
